spacecraft to visit the most distant <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_giant\">ice giant planet</a>. Based on the images recorded during its close encounter and in the following days, <a href=\"https://www.rolfolsenastrophotography.com/Astrophotography/Solar-System/i-vjMHSxz\">this inspired composited scene</a> covers the dim outer planet, largest <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-june-23-flying-past-neptunes-moon-triton/\">moon Triton</a>, and faint system of rings. Parts of the <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rings_of_Neptune\">very faint ring system</a> along with the three bright ring arcs were first imaged by Voyager during the fly-by, though the faintest segments are modeled in this composited picture. Spanning 7.5 degrees, the background starfield is composed from sky survey data centered on the constellation Camelopardalis, corresponding to the outbound Voyager's view of the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/neptune/\">magnificent Neptunian system</a>. Still cruising in 2026, the Voyager 2 spacecraft is <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/where-are-voyager-1-and-voyager-2-now/\">now in interstellar space</a>.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>swirling\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-22-swirls-and-colors-on-jupiter-from-juno/\">APOD: 2026 November 22 \u2013 Swirls and Colors on Jupiter from Juno</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-20-v-g-r/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-22-swirls-and-colors-on-jupiter-from-juno/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nJerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. A small, dark nebula near the center looks like a horse&#039;s head.\"></a>\n</center>\n\n<center>\n<b> The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas </b> <br>\n\n<b>Image Credit &\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Copyright</a>:</b>\n\n<a href=\"https://www.pop-imagery.com/\">Mark E. Killion</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> Today's <a href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/i/ju7bwr?r=B\">image</a> could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-november-20-alnitak-alnilam-mintaka/\">Alnitak</a> (the Girdle): <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alnitak\">a triple star system</a> best known for being the easternmost star in <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stories/quick-reads/discovering-the-universe-through-the-constellation-orion/\">Orion's Belt</a>. The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse's head at the center is the aptly named <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-september-2-the-horsehead-and-flame-nebulas/\">Horsehead Nebula</a>. It is about five light-years tall and lies approximately 1,500 light-years away. It is made of <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-december-10-the-horsehead-nebula/\">dust and gas</a> that obscure the red glow behind it, which is caused by hydrogen gas being ionized by the bright star <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_Orionis\">Sigma Orionis</a> at the top. The orange nebula with dark filaments on the left is the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flame_Nebula\">Flame Nebula</a>. Closer to the Horsehead, the blue <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stories/quick-reads/decoding-nebulae/\">reflection nebula</a> <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-november-20-the-horsehead-nebula/\">NGC 2023</a> is actively forming stars. The data for this \"painting\" were collected for almost six hours at the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah\">Utah</a> <a href=\"https://utahdesertremote.com/\">Desert Remote Observatories</a>, but the equipment was <a href=\"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1596965349990-6d67ce6b0c1c\">remotely controlled</a> by the astrophotographer from his home, over 2,000 km away in <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois\">Illinois</a>.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> V-G-R\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-20-v-g-r/\">APOD: 2026 November 20 \u2013 V-G-R</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-18-an-m-class-solar-flare/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-20-v-g-r/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nCecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. Today\u2019s image combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the Sun\u2019s chromosphere, the layer of the Sun\u2019s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises. Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun\u2019s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap, releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare. The H-alpha filter used for today\u2019s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun\u2019s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations, meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays. M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth\u2019s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren\u2019t even the most powerful flares! NASA, NOAA, and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space.Tomorrow&#039;s picture: a horse of a different color\">\n<!-- -->\n<meta name=\"keywords\" content=\"a medium-sized solar flare\">\n<meta property=\"og:type\" content=\"article\">\n<meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"A Medium-Sized Solar Flare\">\n<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-18-an-m-class-solar-flare/\">\n<meta property=\"og:site_name\" content=\"NASA Science\">\n<meta property=\"og:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/solar_M_flare.jpg?w=3000&#038;h=2759&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:secure_url\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/solar_M_flare.jpg?w=3000&#038;h=2759&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:alt\" content=\"A piece of the Sun takes up half the image. The Sun looks fuzzy and swirling with energetic hydrogen atoms. A bright and dark spot are visible on the Sun, associated with a sun spot. A wisp of hydrogen reaches off of the edge of the Sun.\"></a>\n</center>\n\n<center>\n<b> A Medium-Sized Solar Flare </b> <br>\n\n<b>Image Credit &\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Copyright</a>:</b>\n\n<a href=\"https://www.facebook.com/mario.cogo.9\">Mario Cogo</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> What a <a href=\"https://idioms.thefreedictionary.com/flair+for+the+dramatic\">flare for the chromatic</a>! <a href=\"http://galaxlux.com/Sun-%20Solar%20Limb%20Dynamics%2014%20May%202025.htm\">Today\u2019s image</a> combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/sun/\">Sun</a>\u2019s <a href=\"https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/sun-space-weather/chromosphere\">chromosphere</a>, the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/the-sun-spot/2023/09/26/layers-of-the-sun/\">layer of the Sun</a>\u2019s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature <em>rises</em>. Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/sun-heat/en/\">core</a>? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling <a href=\"https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/the_key.shtml\">magnetic fields</a> extending up through the Sun\u2019s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can <a href=\"https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/20310#media_group_320369\">twist and snap</a>, releasing light and energetic particles as a <a href=\"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oOXVZo7KikE\">solar flare</a>. The <a href=\"https://skyandtelescope.org/stargazing-and-observing/guide-to-observing-the-sun-in-h-alpha092321050923/\">H-alpha filter</a> used for today\u2019s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun\u2019s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was <a href=\"https://solar-center.stanford.edu/sid/activities/flare.html\">classified</a> as an M1 based on <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/goes/\">GOES</a> <a href=\"https://www.spaceweatherlive.com/en/archive/2025/05/14/xray.html\">observations</a>, meaning it was moderately bright in <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/ems/11_xrays/\">X-rays</a>. M-class flares can cause <a href=\"https://www.spaceweather.gov/phenomena/solar-flares-radio-blackouts\">radio blackouts</a> at Earth\u2019s poles and minor <a href=\"https://www.spaceweather.gov/phenomena/solar-radiation-storm\">radiation storms</a> that can harm astronauts. They aren\u2019t even <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2018-september-2-a-powerful-solar-flare/\">the most powerful flares</a>! NASA, <a href=\"https://www.noaa.gov/\">NOAA</a>, and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> a horse of a different color\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-19-the-horsehead-and-flame-nebulas/\">APOD: 2026 November 19 &#8211; The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-17-milky-way-versus-aurora/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-19-the-horsehead-and-flame-nebulas/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nKeighley Rockcliffe, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. No, but it sure looks like it! The arch on the left is the central band of our\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/resource/the-milky-way-galaxy/\">Milky Way Galaxy</a>, an ancient system of stars, gas, and dust that predates\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/resource/planet-earth-through-the-ages/\">our Earth</a>\u00a0and is very far away. The arch on the right, by contrast, is an\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2004-november-12-missouris-green-ribbon-sky/\">auroral ribbon</a>\u00a0that is only hours old, composed of energized\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/articles/zc86m39#zygjdp3\">atoms and molecules</a>, and is close by -- right in\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/properties-of-earths-upper-atmosphere/\">Earth's upper atmosphere</a>. These chance-superposed\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-november-30-the-surface-of-titan-from-huygens/\">titan</a>s have\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-june-15-prominences-and-filaments-on-the-active-sun/\">our Sun</a>\u00a0in common, a\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.reddit.com/media?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpreview.redd.it%2Fthis-is-the-most-cute-thing-i-ever-seen-v0-mpx697lakcue1.jpg%3Fwidth%3D1080%26crop%3Dsmart%26auto%3Dwebp%26s%3Da5d18b145135737912b5caa61fcc56766726f6cb\">stellar member</a>\u00a0of the\u00a0Milky Way\u00a0that ejects energetic particles which create\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-february-10-in-green-company-aurora-over-norway/\">aurora</a>s. Far behind the middle of the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2021-january-13-arches-across-an-arctic-sky/\">auroral arch</a>\u00a0is the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2013-april-21-the-big-dipper/\">Big Dipper</a>. Even farther in the distance is the\u00a0<a href=\"https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11675/\">Andromeda galaxy</a>\u00a0-- the bright spot near the top of the frame, just left of center. The\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/p/DfAZEgmIDIq/\">featured image</a>\u00a0was taken about a month ago from\u00a0<a href=\"https://youtu.be/4VlzJh3WBGU\">Kval\u00f8ya</a>\u00a0in northern\u00a0<a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway\">Norway</a>.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:\u00a0</strong>open space\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-18-an-m-class-solar-flare/\">APOD: 2026 November 18 &#8211; A Medium-Sized Solar Flare</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-16-ngc-7129-star-formation-with-jets-from-webb/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-18-an-m-class-solar-flare/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nRobert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light. Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds -- and some then explode. Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image, with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right -- in the red region. Jets and winds likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when.Tomorrow&#039;s picture: sky duel\">\n<!-- -->\n<meta name=\"keywords\" content=\"ngc 7129: star formation with jets from webb\">\n<meta property=\"og:type\" content=\"article\">\n<meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb\">\n<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-16-ngc-7129-star-formation-with-jets-from-webb/\">\n<meta property=\"og:site_name\" content=\"NASA Science\">\n<meta property=\"og:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/missions/webb/science/2026/10/weic2620a.jpg?w=1280&#038;h=1194&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:secure_url\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/missions/webb/science/2026/10/weic2620a.jpg?w=1280&#038;h=1194&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:alt\" content=\"A young star cluster filled with many stars that display Webb\u2019s unique eight-pronged diffraction pattern. At its center is a yellow star that sports the largest diffraction pattern. To its left, there is a region filled with yellow dust and gas that extends from the star to the left and the bottom, covering about two-thirds of the frame. The yellow region has several embedded blue stars of different sizes. The top third, which lies outside the yellow region, has a few bright protostars, within dense gray gas. These stars illuminate the gas, making it appear blue. A few red outflows from other protostars are visible above this grayish-blue region. To the right of the central star, there is a clumpy, flame-like plume of red dust and gas with protostars that emit a soft white light within. The plume is surrounded by more dense gray gas and dust. It is about one third the size of the yellow region. There are several background galaxies strewn throughout.\">\n<meta property=\"article:published_time\" content=\"2026-11-16T00:05:00-05:00\">\n<meta property=\"article:modified_time\" content=\"2026-11-15T20:23:37-05:00\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:card\" content=\"summary_large_image\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:title\" content=\"NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:site\" content=\"@NASA\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:creator\" content=\"@NASA\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/missions/webb/science/2026/10/weic2620a.jpg?w=1280&#038;h=1194&#038;fit=clip\">\n</head>\n<body BGCOLOR=\"#F4F4FF\" text=\"#000000\" link=\"#0000FF\" vlink=\"#7F0F9F\"\nalink=\"#FF0000\">\n\n<center>\n<h1> Astronomy Picture of the Day </h1>\n<p>\n\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Discover the cosmos!</a>\nEach day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is\nfeatured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.\n<p>\n\n2026 November 16<br>\n\n<a href=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/missions/webb/science/2026/10/weic2620a.jpg\">\n<IMG SRC=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/missions/webb/science/2026/10/weic2620a.jpg\" alt=\"A young star cluster filled with many stars that display Webb\u2019s unique eight-pronged diffraction pattern. The yellow region has several embedded blue stars of different sizes. The top third, which lies outside the yellow region, has a few bright protostars, within dense gray gas. Pagan</a> (<a href=\"https://www.stsci.edu/\">STScI</a>)\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> How do stars form? To help answer this question, <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> used the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/\">James Webb Space Telescope</a> to take the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/ngc-7129-nircam-image/\">featured detailed image</a> of the star-forming region <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGC_7129\">NGC 7129</a> in <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/ems/07_infraredwaves/\">infrared light</a>. Star formation progresses when <a href=\"https://www.labxchange.org/library/items/lb:LabXchange:bc30bab5:lx_simulation:1\">gravity</a> pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-july-28-young-stars-stellar-jets/\">jets</a> and <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-february-3-wolf-rayet-star-124-stellar-wind-machine/\">winds</a> -- and some then <a href=\"https://youtu.be/-yEBVm5o97E\">explode</a>. Opaque <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/universe/dust-in-the-stellar-wind-a-cosmological-primer/\">dust</a> can form in the cool <a href=\"https://www.eso.org/sci/meetings/2024/Bthelines/Ludwig.pdf\">atmospheres of stars</a> and, when dispersed, can obstruct <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/ems/09_visiblelight/\">visible-light</a> images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/ngc-7129-nircam-image/#:~:text=Interactive:\">featured image</a>, with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right -- in the red region. <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-may-28-herbig-haro-24/\">Jets</a> and <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2000-march-18-a-wind-from-the-sun/\">wind</a>s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development <a href=\"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1734167121479-6147220c23f0?q=80&amp;w=687&amp;auto=format&amp;fit=crop&amp;ixlib=rb-4.1.0&amp;ixid=NHwxMjA3fDA%3D\">bolsters understanding</a> about what <a href=\"https://scixplorer.org/abs/2020SSRv..216...68G/abstract\">physical processes</a> are most important and when.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> sky duel\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-17-milky-way-versus-aurora/\">APOD: 2026 November 17 &#8211; Milky Way versus Aurora</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-15-leonid-meteors-through-orion/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-17-milky-way-versus-aurora/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nRobert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. Even during a meteor shower, it is practically impossible to know. Therefore, a good way to enjoy a <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/meteor-shower/\">meteor shower</a> is to find a place where you can sit comfortably and monitor a great expanse of dark sky. And it may be satisfying to share this experience with a friend. The meteor shower depicted was the 2022 <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/leonids/\">Leonids</a> and the view is from <a href=\"https://youtu.be/GANaIlOIjvA\">Hainan</a>, <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China\">China</a> looking out over the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea\">South China Sea</a>. Meteor streaks captured over a few hours were isolated and added to a foreground image recorded earlier. <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-1998-december-08-leonids-from-leo/\">Leonid meteor streaks</a> trace back to the <a href=\"https://earthsky.org/constellations/leo-heres-your-constellation/\">constellation of Leo</a> and were here seen <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2018-november-23-good-morning-leonid/\">streaking across</a> the constellation of Orion. The bright red <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mars/facts/\">planet Mars</a> appears near the top of the image. The <a href=\"https://www.planetary.org/articles/your-guide-meteor-shower\">Leonids peak</a> in mid-November every year and so will <a href=\"https://www.cuteness.com/img/gallery/15-funny-photos-that-are-peak-cat/intro-1762504825.webp\">peak again</a> this week. Bonding over their love of astronomy, the two pictured meteor enthusiasts, shown celebrating their <a href=\"https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/bring-science-home-probability-birthday-paradox/\">common birthday</a> this month, were later married.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong><a href=\"https://apod.com/fap/ap261116.html\">open space</a>","credit":"<a href=\"mailto:mgsluo at gmail dot com\">Luo Hongyang</a>","copyright":"<a href=\"mailto:mgsluo at gmail dot com\">Luo Hongyang</a>","alt":"A composite showing many meteors trails streaking across a sky featuring the familiar constellation of Orion. Please see the explanation for more detailed information.","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-15-leonid-meteors-through-orion/","hdurl":"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/Leonids2022_Hongyang_2880.jpg?w=2880&h=3600&fit=clip","basic_html":"<!doctype html>\n<html>\n<head>\n<meta charset=\"UTF-8\">\n<meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">\n<title> APOD: 2026 November 15 - Leonid Meteors Through Orion</title>\n<link rel=\"canonical\" href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-15-leonid-meteors-through-orion/\">\n<!-- gsfc meta tags -->\n<meta name=\"orgcode\" content=\"661\">\n<meta name=\"rno\" content=\"Dana Bolles\">\n<meta name=\"content-owner\" content=\"Robert Nemiroff\">\n<meta name=\"webmaster\" content=\"Stephen.F.Fantasia.1\">\n<meta name=\"description\" content=\"Explanation: Where will the next meteor appear? Even during a meteor shower, it is practically impossible to know. Therefore, a good way to enjoy a meteor shower is to find a place where you can sit comfortably and monitor a great expanse of dark sky. And it may be satisfying to share this experience with a friend. The meteor shower depicted was the 2022 Leonids and the view is from Hainan, China looking out over the South China Sea. Meteor streaks captured over a few hours were isolated and added to a foreground image recorded earlier. Leonid meteor streaks trace back to the constellation of Leo and were here seen streaking across the constellation of Orion. The bright red planet Mars appears near the top of the image. The Leonids peak in mid-November every year and so will peak again this week. Bonding over their love of astronomy, the two pictured meteor enthusiasts, shown celebrating their common birthday this month, were later married.Tomorrow&#039;s picture: open space\">\n<!-- -->\n<meta name=\"keywords\" content=\"leonid meteors through orion\">\n<meta property=\"og:type\" content=\"article\">\n<meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"Leonid Meteors Through Orion\">\n<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-15-leonid-meteors-through-orion/\">\n<meta property=\"og:site_name\" content=\"NASA Science\">\n<meta property=\"og:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/Leonids2022_Hongyang_2880.jpg?w=2880&#038;h=3600&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:secure_url\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/Leonids2022_Hongyang_2880.jpg?w=2880&#038;h=3600&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:alt\" content=\"A composite showing many meteors trails streaking across a sky featuring the familiar constellation of Orion. In the foreground two people sit in adjoining chairs facing away from the camera, one holding a wand with a glowing star at the end. Please see the explanation for more detailed information.\"></a>\n</center>\n\n<center>\n<b> Leonid Meteors Through Orion </b> <br>\n\n<b>Image Credit &\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Copyright</a>:</b>\n\n<a href=\"mailto:mgsluo at gmail dot com\">Luo Hongyang</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> Where will the next meteor appear? Even during a meteor shower, it is practically impossible to know. Therefore, a good way to enjoy a <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/meteor-shower/\">meteor shower</a> is to find a place where you can sit comfortably and monitor a great expanse of dark sky. And it may be satisfying to share this experience with a friend. The meteor shower depicted was the 2022 <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/leonids/\">Leonids</a> and the view is from <a href=\"https://youtu.be/GANaIlOIjvA\">Hainan</a>, <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China\">China</a> looking out over the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea\">South China Sea</a>. Meteor streaks captured over a few hours were isolated and added to a foreground image recorded earlier. <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-1998-december-08-leonids-from-leo/\">Leonid meteor streaks</a> trace back to the <a href=\"https://earthsky.org/constellations/leo-heres-your-constellation/\">constellation of Leo</a> and were here seen <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2018-november-23-good-morning-leonid/\">streaking across</a> the constellation of Orion. The bright red <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mars/facts/\">planet Mars</a> appears near the top of the image. The <a href=\"https://www.planetary.org/articles/your-guide-meteor-shower\">Leonids peak</a> in mid-November every year and so will <a href=\"https://www.cuteness.com/img/gallery/15-funny-photos-that-are-peak-cat/intro-1762504825.webp\">peak again</a> this week. Bonding over their love of astronomy, the two pictured meteor enthusiasts, shown celebrating their <a href=\"https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/bring-science-home-probability-birthday-paradox/\">common birthday</a> this month, were later married.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong><a href=\"https://apod.com/fap/ap261116.html\">open space</a>\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-16-ngc-7129-star-formation-with-jets-from-webb/\">APOD: 2026 November 16 &#8211; NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-14-apollo-12-and-surveyor-3/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-16-ngc-7129-star-formation-with-jets-from-webb/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nRobert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. Also known as M31, <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-shows-milky-way-is-destined-for-head-on-collision/\">the spiral galaxy is a mere</a> 2.5 million light-years away. NGC 206 is found at the center of <a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/astro.midnight/p/DfmV8AJjmn-/\">this sharp and detailed close-up</a> of the southwestern <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=200925\">extent</a> of Andromeda's disk. The bright, blue <a href=\"https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010MNRAS.405.1531E/abstract\">stars of NGC 206</a> indicate its youth. In fact, its youngest massive stars are less than 10 million years old. galaxy.\"></a>\n</center>\n\n<center>\n<b> NGC 206 and the Star Clouds of Andromeda </b> <br>\n\n<b>Image Credit &\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Copyright</a>:</b>\n\n<a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/astro.midnight\">David Cruz</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> The large stellar association cataloged as <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=990402\">NGC 206</a> is nestled within the dusty arms of the neighboring <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=220119\">Andromeda galaxy</a> along with the galaxy's pinkish star-forming regions. Also known as M31, <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-shows-milky-way-is-destined-for-head-on-collision/\">the spiral galaxy is a mere</a> 2.5 million light-years away. NGC 206 is found at the center of <a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/astro.midnight/p/DfmV8AJjmn-/\">this sharp and detailed close-up</a> of the southwestern <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=200925\">extent</a> of Andromeda's disk. The bright, blue <a href=\"https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010MNRAS.405.1531E/abstract\">stars of NGC 206</a> indicate its youth. In fact, its youngest massive stars are less than 10 million years old. Much larger than the open or galactic clusters of young stars <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=120912\">in the disk</a><a> of our Milky Way galaxy, </a><a href=\"http://messier.seds.org/more/m031_n206.html\">NGC 206</a> spans about 4,000 light-years. That's comparable in size to the giant stellar nurseries <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=240425\">NGC 604</a> in nearby spiral M33 and the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=240308\">Tarantula Nebula</a> in the Large Magellanic Cloud.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>pixels on the Moon\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-14-apollo-12-and-surveyor-3/\">APOD: 2026 November 14 \u2013 Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-12-moon-venus-and-spica-meet/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-14-apollo-12-and-surveyor-3/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nJerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. The bright star to the left of Venus is Spica in the constellation of Virgo, the Maiden. Spica is one of the brightest stars in the sky, only about 250 light-years away. href=\"https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Riddle_of_Strider\">Not all those who wander are lost.</a> A night sky example is that <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/\">planets</a> wander, and in fact the very word \"planet\" comes from \"wandering star\" in Greek. As planets <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-may-30-mars-in-the-loop/\">shift</a> relative to <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/planetary-motion/\">fixed stars</a>, they may appear from our perspective to <a href=\"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1504595403659-9088ce801e29\">get closer</a> to other astronomical objects. Such <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-march-4-10-days-of-venus-and-jupiter/\">meetings</a> are called <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2020-december-15-great-conjunction-saturn-and-jupiter-converge/\">conjunctions</a>. They don't happen by chance, but follow the precise laws of <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/orbits-and-keplers-laws/\">celestial mechanics</a>. This peaceful <a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/p/DfciOD3DKOE/?img_index=1\">image</a>, captured in  <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland\">Poland</a>, shows the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-april-24-young-moon-and-sister-stars/\">crescent Moon</a> above the <a href=\"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x1YiJgA8lpw\">Tatra Mountains</a>, and bright <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/venus/\">Venus</a> close by, a little lower in the horizon. The bright star to the left of Venus is <a href=\"https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/news/understanding-spica\">Spica</a> in the constellation of <a href=\"https://noirlab.edu/public/education/constellations/virgo/\">Virgo</a>, the Maiden. Spica is <a href=\"https://earthsky.org/brightest-stars/speed-on-to-spica-the-15th-brightest-star/\">one of the brightest stars</a> in the sky, only about 250 light-years away. It was found in 1890 that <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spica\">Spica</a> is a binary star: two massive blue stars orbiting each other every 4 days. But earlier this year it was reported that Spica, the current companion of wandering Venus, is actually a <a href=\"https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/2515-5172/aea83b\">triple system</a>.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> what's next?\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-13-ngc-206-and-the-star-clouds-of-andromeda/\">APOD: 2026 November 13 \u2013 NGC 206 and the Star Clouds of Andromeda</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-11-ngc-4449-small-galaxy-big-impact/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-13-ngc-206-and-the-star-clouds-of-andromeda/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nCecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. Our home galaxy, the <a href=\"http://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/features/cosmic/milkyway_info.html\">Milky Way</a>, is about 100,000 <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanets/what-is-a-light-year/\">light years</a> across. This huge expanse of space contains hundreds of billions of stars! The smallest galaxies, called <a href=\"https://esahubble.org/wordbank/dwarf-galaxy/\">dwarf galaxies</a>, are about 1/10th the size of the Milky Way and only contain a few billion stars. They are also the <a href=\"https://www.eso.org/public/blog/little-galaxies-big-mysteries/\">most common type of galaxy</a> in the whole universe. <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/asset/hubble/dwarf-galaxy-ngc-4449/\">Today\u2019s image</a> shows one such dwarf galaxy, <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2017-july-14-ngc-4449-close-up-of-a-small-galaxy/\">NGC 4449</a>, captured by the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/\">Hubble Space Telescope</a>. NGC 4449 and similar dwarf galaxies are <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-uncovers-case-of-missing-oxygen-in-nearby-dwarf-galaxies/\">missing more oxygen</a> than models predict. This suggests their <a href=\"https://esahubble.org/wordbank/stellar-wind/\">stellar winds</a> and <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/supernova/en/\">supernovae</a> are surprisingly effective at <a href=\"https://tenor.com/dLL7CwmYnWj.gif\">blowing away</a> oxygen and other heavy elements. This suggests their stellar winds and supernovae are surprisingly effective at blowing away oxygen and other heavy elements. This huge expanse of space contains hundreds of billions of stars! The smallest galaxies, called <a href=\"https://esahubble.org/wordbank/dwarf-galaxy/\">dwarf galaxies</a>, are about 1/10th the size of the Milky Way and only contain a few billion stars. They are also the <a href=\"https://www.eso.org/public/blog/little-galaxies-big-mysteries/\">most common type of galaxy</a> in the whole universe. <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/asset/hubble/dwarf-galaxy-ngc-4449/\">Today\u2019s image</a> shows one such dwarf galaxy, <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2017-july-14-ngc-4449-close-up-of-a-small-galaxy/\">NGC 4449</a>, captured by the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/\">Hubble Space Telescope</a>. NGC 4449 and similar dwarf galaxies are <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-uncovers-case-of-missing-oxygen-in-nearby-dwarf-galaxies/\">missing more oxygen</a> than models predict. This suggests their <a href=\"https://esahubble.org/wordbank/stellar-wind/\">stellar winds</a> and <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/supernova/en/\">supernovae</a> are surprisingly effective at <a href=\"https://tenor.com/dLL7CwmYnWj.gif\">blowing away</a> oxygen and other heavy elements. Turns out these tiny galaxies may play a big role in spreading heavy elements \u2014 the building blocks of stars, planets, and life \u2014 throughout the universe!<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> a date in Poland\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-12-moon-venus-and-spica-meet/\">APOD: 2026 November 12 &#8211; Moon, Venus and Spica Meet</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-10-saturn-behind-the-moon/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-12-moon-venus-and-spica-meet/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nKeighley Rockcliffe, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. To the upper right of the star is an unusually shaped blue-tinted nebula.\"></a>\n</center>\n\n<center>\n<b> Rigel and the Witch Head Nebula </b> <br>\n\n<b>Image Credit &\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Copyright</a>:</b>\n\n<a href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/u/PiotrC\">Piotr Czerski</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> Does the blue nebula look like the head of a witch? The nebula is <a href=\"https://earthsky.org/todays-image/witch-head-nebula-orion/\">known popularly</a> as the Witch Head Nebula because, it is said, the nebula's shape resembles a <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween#/media/File:Halloween_Witch_2011.JPG\">Halloween-style caricature</a> of a witch's head. Exactly how, though, can be a topic of <a href=\"https://unsplash.com/photos/a-cat-wearing-glasses-and-a-jacket-on-a-rug-nzfEUQrZZGc\">imaginative speculation</a>. What is clear is that <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IC_2118\">IC 2118</a> is about 50 <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/light-year/\">light-years</a> across and made of gas and dust that points to -- because it has been partly eroded by -- the nearby star <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigel\">Rigel</a>. One of the brighter stars in the constellation Orion, <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-april-7-rigel-wide/\">Rigel</a> lies just below the center of the <a href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/u/PiotrC?i=ttmxgn\">featured image</a>. The blue color of the Witch Head Nebula and is caused not only by <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-may-8-comet-r3-panstarrs-before-rigel/\">Rigel's intense blue starlight</a> but also because the <a href=\"https://curator.jsc.nasa.gov/dust/\">dust grains</a> scatter blue light more efficiently than red. The same <a href=\"http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/atmos/blusky.html\">physical process</a> causes Earth's daytime <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/blue-sky/en/\">sky to appear blue</a>, although the scatterers in planet <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-atmosphere/earths-atmosphere-a-multi-layered-cake/\">Earth's atmosphere</a> are molecules of <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/nasas-curiosity-rover-finds-biologically-useful-nitrogen-on-mars/\">nitrogen</a> and <a href=\"https://astrobiology.nasa.gov/news/lightning-oxygen-and-life-detection/\">oxygen</a>.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> suddenly Saturn\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-10-saturn-behind-the-moon/\">APOD: 2026 November 10 &#8211; Saturn Behind the Moon</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-8-major-fireball-meteor/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-10-saturn-behind-the-moon/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nRobert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. Taken in subfreezing temperatures, the <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2017/11/Autumn_fireball\">thoughtfully composed photo</a> shows snowy, rugged peaks seen from a mountain pass on 2017 November 14. Below lies the village of <a href=\"https://youtu.be/bVNV2-wma5E\">La Villa, Alta Badia</a> in <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy\">Italy</a>'s <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-november-6-comet-tsuchinshan-atlas-over-the-dolomites/\">Dolomite Alps</a>. It was <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2017/11/Autumn_fireball\">captured</a> during the camera's exposure by chance as it flashed east to west across the northern horizon, under Ursa Major's familiar <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2013-april-21-the-big-dipper/\">Big Dipper</a> <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/what-are-asterisms/\">asterism</a>. Taken in subfreezing temperatures, the thoughtfully composed photo shows snowy, rugged peaks seen from a mountain pass on 2017 November 14. Below lies the village of La Villa, Alta Badia in Italy&#039;s Dolomite Alps. Above the nestled village lights, the constellation Ursa Major hangs over the northern horizon. But most stunning is the intense fireball meteor. It was captured during the camera&#039;s exposure by chance as it flashed east to west across the northern horizon, under Ursa Major&#039;s familiar Big Dipper asterism. Sightings of this major fireball meteor were widely reported in European skies, making it one of the most reported fireball events ever for planet Earth&#039;s American Meteor Society and the International Meteor Organization. The meteor&#039;s measured track over Germany is consistent with its origin near the active radiant of November&#039;s Northern Taurid Meteor Shower, a shower associated with dust from Encke&#039;s comet.Tomorrow&#039;s picture: witch sky?\">\n<!-- -->\n<meta name=\"keywords\" content=\"major fireball meteor\">\n<meta property=\"og:type\" content=\"article\">\n<meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"Major Fireball Meteor\">\n<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-8-major-fireball-meteor/\">\n<meta property=\"og:site_name\" content=\"NASA Science\">\n<meta property=\"og:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/content/dam/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/meteor2017_Taylor_1200.jpg/jcr:content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.48.48.png\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:secure_url\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/content/dam/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/meteor2017_Taylor_1200.jpg/jcr:content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.48.48.png\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:alt\" content=\"A mountainous landscape with snow and trees is seen  below a starry sky. A pink band is visible on the horizon.  Coming down from the sky is a bright meteor trail. Just above the meteor are the stars of the Big Dipper.  Please see the explanation for more detailed information.\">\n<meta property=\"article:published_time\" content=\"2026-11-08T00:05:00-05:00\">\n<meta property=\"article:modified_time\" content=\"2026-11-04T10:32:05-05:00\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:card\" content=\"summary_large_image\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:title\" content=\"Major Fireball Meteor\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:site\" content=\"@NASA\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:creator\" content=\"@NASA\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/content/dam/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/meteor2017_Taylor_1200.jpg/jcr:content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.48.48.png\">\n</head>\n<body BGCOLOR=\"#F4F4FF\" text=\"#000000\" link=\"#0000FF\" vlink=\"#7F0F9F\"\nalink=\"#FF0000\">\n\n<center>\n<h1> Astronomy Picture of the Day </h1>\n<p>\n\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Discover the cosmos!</a>\nEach day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is\nfeatured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.\n<p>\n\n2026 November 8<br>\n\n<a href=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/meteor2017_Taylor_1200.jpg\">\n<IMG SRC=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/meteor2017_Taylor_1200.jpg\" alt=\"A mountainous landscape with snow and trees is seen  below a starry sky. A pink band is visible on the horizon.  Coming down from the sky is a bright meteor trail. Just above the meteor are the stars of the Big Dipper.  Please see the explanation for more detailed information.\"></a>\n</center>\n\n<center>\n<b> Major Fireball Meteor </b> <br>\n\n<b>Image Credit &\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Copyright</a>:</b>\n\n<a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/olliemtaylor/\">Ollie Taylor</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2010-july-22-the-meteor-of-1860/\">The sky glows</a> with soft pinkish colors of fading twilight in this serendipitous mountaintop vista. Taken in subfreezing temperatures, the <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2017/11/Autumn_fireball\">thoughtfully composed photo</a> shows snowy, rugged peaks seen from a mountain pass on 2017 November 14. Below lies the village of <a href=\"https://youtu.be/bVNV2-wma5E\">La Villa, Alta Badia</a> in <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy\">Italy</a>'s <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-november-6-comet-tsuchinshan-atlas-over-the-dolomites/\">Dolomite Alps</a>. Above the nestled village lights, the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/asset/hubble/constellation-ursa-major/\">constellation Ursa Major</a> hangs over the northern horizon. But most <a href=\"https://unsplash.com/photos/white-and-gray-long-fur-cat-AGehl6k8xVo\">stunning</a> is the intense <a href=\"https://cneos.jpl.nasa.gov/fireballs/intro.html\">fireball</a> meteor. It was <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2017/11/Autumn_fireball\">captured</a> during the camera's exposure by chance as it flashed east to west across the northern horizon, under Ursa Major's familiar <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2013-april-21-the-big-dipper/\">Big Dipper</a> <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/what-are-asterisms/\">asterism</a>. Sightings of <a href=\"https://www.amsmeteors.org/2017/11/four-major-fireballs-within-ten-hours/\">this major fireball meteor</a> were widely reported in European skies, making it one of the most reported fireball events ever for planet Earth's <a href=\"https://www.amsmeteors.org/\">American Meteor Society</a> and the <a href=\"https://www.imo.net/\">International Meteor Organization</a>. The meteor's measured track over <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany\">Germany</a> is consistent with its origin near the active <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-august-12-perseids-from-perseus/\">radiant</a> of November's Northern <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-august-12-perseids-from-perseus/\">Taurid Meteor Shower</a>, a shower associated with dust from <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2003-december-23-comet-encke-returns/\">Encke's comet</a>.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> witch sky?\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-9-rigel-and-the-witch-head-nebula/\">APOD: 2026 November 9 &#8211; Rigel and the Witch Head Nebula</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-7-de-gerlache-kocher-massif/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-9-rigel-and-the-witch-head-nebula/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nRobert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. U.</a><br>\n</center>\n</body>\n</html>","basic_html_url":"https://science.nasa.gov/wp-json/wp/v2/apod-basic/261108/html"},{"date":"2026-11-07","post_id":1509014,"title":"De Gerlache-Kocher Massif","permalink":"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-7-de-gerlache-kocher-massif/","media_type":"image","explanation":"<strong>Explanation:</strong> De Gerlache-Kocher <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif\">massif</a> looms on the visible horizon in this close-up of the edge of the Moon. The mountainous formation rises about 4 kilometers above its surroundings and is located very close to the lunar south pole. Boasting <a href=\"https://lroc.im-ldi.com/images/271\">permanently shadowed</a> crater floors that likely contain deposits of water ice and peaks that receive almost continuous sunlight for solar power generation, the south polar region is <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase/\">considered a prime location</a> for the first human settlement on the Moon. <a href=\"https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023LPICo2989.2037E/abstract\">In fact</a>, De Gerlache-Kocher massif itself has been considered as a potential <a href=\"https://www.universetoday.com/articles/nasa-narrows-artemis-landing-sites-to-9-key-regions\">landing site</a> for future crewed <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-iv/\">Artemis missions to the Moon</a>. The remarkable telescopic image of the massif at the lunar limb was captured on October 31. Then, a favorable libration angle or <a href=\"https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/10836/\">lunar wobble</a> enhanced this oblique view <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-august-30-southern-moonscape/\">across the Moon's south pole.</a><br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>meteoric","credit":"<a href=\"https://www.flickr.com/photos/204361611@N08/\">Alejandro Sanz</a>","copyright":"<a href=\"https://www.flickr.com/photos/204361611@N08/\">Alejandro Sanz</a>","alt":"Mountains and craters at the lunar limb.","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-7-de-gerlache-kocher-massif/","hdurl":"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/GerlacheKocherMassif_Sans.jpg?w=1500&h=1022&fit=clip","basic_html":"<!doctype html>\n<html>\n<head>\n<meta charset=\"UTF-8\">\n<meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">\n<title> APOD: 2026 November 7 - De Gerlache-Kocher Massif</title>\n<link rel=\"canonical\" href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-7-de-gerlache-kocher-massif/\">\n<!-- gsfc meta tags -->\n<meta name=\"orgcode\" content=\"661\">\n<meta name=\"rno\" content=\"Dana Bolles\">\n<meta name=\"content-owner\" content=\"Robert Nemiroff\">\n<meta name=\"webmaster\" content=\"Stephen.F.Fantasia.1\">\n<meta name=\"description\" content=\"Explanation: De Gerlache-Kocher massif looms on the visible horizon in this close-up of the edge of the Moon. Boasting permanently shadowed crater floors that likely contain deposits of water ice and peaks that receive almost continuous sunlight for solar power generation, the south polar region is considered a prime location for the first human settlement on the Moon. In fact, De Gerlache-Kocher massif itself has been considered as a potential landing site for future crewed Artemis missions to the Moon. The remarkable telescopic image of the massif at the lunar limb was captured on October 31. text=\"#000000\" link=\"#0000FF\" vlink=\"#7F0F9F\"\nalink=\"#FF0000\">\n\n<center>\n<h1> Astronomy Picture of the Day </h1>\n<p>\n\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Discover the cosmos!</a>\nEach day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is\nfeatured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.\n<p>\n\n2026 November 7<br>\n\n<a SRC=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/GerlacheKocherMassif_Sans.jpg\" alt=\"Mountains and craters at the lunar href=\"https://www.flickr.com/photos/204361611@N08/\">Alejandro Sanz</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> De Gerlache-Kocher <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif\">massif</a> looms on the visible horizon in this close-up of the edge of the Moon. The mountainous formation rises about 4 kilometers above its surroundings and is located very close to the lunar south pole. Boasting <a href=\"https://lroc.im-ldi.com/images/271\">permanently shadowed</a> crater floors that likely contain deposits of water ice and peaks that receive almost continuous sunlight for solar power generation, the south polar region is <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase/\">considered a prime location</a> for the first human settlement on the Moon. <a href=\"https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023LPICo2989.2037E/abstract\">In fact</a>, De Gerlache-Kocher massif itself has been considered as a potential <a href=\"https://www.universetoday.com/articles/nasa-narrows-artemis-landing-sites-to-9-key-regions\">landing site</a> for future crewed <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-iv/\">Artemis missions to the Moon</a>. The remarkable telescopic image of the massif at the lunar limb was captured on October 31. Then, a favorable libration angle or <a href=\"https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/10836/\">lunar wobble</a> enhanced this oblique view <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-august-30-southern-moonscape/\">across the Moon's south pole.</a><br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>meteoric\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-8-major-fireball-meteor/\">APOD: 2026 November 8 &#8211; Major Fireball Meteor</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-6-a-farewell-to-swift/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-8-major-fireball-meteor/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nJerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. After nearly 22 years of service, the satellite <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/11/02/nasas-swift-observatory-to-re-enter-atmosphere/\">re-entered Earth's atmosphere</a> on November 4 at 7:39 EST over the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sumatra\">North Sumatra</a> region of <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia\">Indonesia</a>. The <a href=\"https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/12980\">featured image</a> is a mosaic created in 2018 using some of the first million <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2009-september-17-ultraviolet-andromeda/\">images</a> captured by the satellite's <a href=\"https://www.swift.psu.edu/uvot/\">Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope</a>. The featured image is a mosaic created in 2018 using some of the first million images captured by the satellite&#039;s Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope. Swift had a combination of instruments, including an X-ray telescope and a gamma-ray telescope, that worked together to enable humanity to study, in unprecedented detail, the fastest and most energetic explosions in the universe. The most recent solar maximum accelerated the decay of the satellite&#039;s orbit. An innovative mission to rescue Swift by boosting its orbit was not successful. Swift burned on reentry like a shooting star, but the impressive data acquired by the telescope over its mission will continue to bring light to the mysteries of the cosmos for years to come. May it keep inspiring new missions to boldly go into space, explore new data and seek out new science. href=\"https://www.andreaplanet.com/andreamosaic/\">AndreaMosaic</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> It is time to say goodbye to <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a>'s <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/swift/\">Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory</a>. After nearly 22 years of service, the satellite <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/11/02/nasas-swift-observatory-to-re-enter-atmosphere/\">re-entered Earth's atmosphere</a> on November 4 at 7:39 EST over the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sumatra\">North Sumatra</a> region of <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia\">Indonesia</a>. The <a href=\"https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/12980\">featured image</a> is a mosaic created in 2018 using some of the first million <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2009-september-17-ultraviolet-andromeda/\">images</a> captured by the satellite's <a href=\"https://www.swift.psu.edu/uvot/\">Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope</a>. Swift had a combination of instruments, including an <a href=\"https://www.swift.psu.edu/xrt/\">X-ray telescope</a> and a <a href=\"https://swift.gsfc.nasa.gov/about_swift/bat_desc.html\">gamma-ray telescope</a>, that worked together to enable humanity to study, in unprecedented detail, the fastest and most energetic <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2022-october-17-x-ray-rings-around-a-gamma-ray-burst/\">explosions</a> in the universe. The most recent <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-february-11-a-year-of-sunspots/\">solar maximum</a> accelerated the decay of the satellite's orbit. An <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/swift/swift-boost-mission/\">innovative mission</a> to <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-july-8-swift-boost-mission/\">rescue Swift</a> by boosting its orbit was <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/\">not successful</a>. Swift burned on <a href=\"https://orbitalradar.com/swift-tracker\">reentry</a> like a shooting star, but the impressive data acquired by the telescope over its mission will continue to bring light to the mysteries of the cosmos for years to come. May it keep inspiring new missions <a href=\"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1501532358732-8b50b34df1c4\">to boldly go</a> into space, explore new data and seek out new science. <br> <br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong>\u00a0Moon Massif\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-7-de-gerlache-kocher-massif/\">APOD: 2026 November 7 \u2013 De Gerlache-Kocher Massif</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-5-enceladus-in-silhouette/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-7-de-gerlache-kocher-massif/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nCecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. They supply material directly to Saturn's outer, tenuous <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=070327\">E ring</a> and make the surface of Enceladus as reflective as snow. Across the scene, Saturn's icy rings scatter sunlight toward Cassini's cameras. Beyond the rings (lower right), the night side of 80 kilometer diameter moon <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=170103\">Pandora</a> is faintly lit by <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=170316\">Saturnlight</a>.<br><br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>pixels in space\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-6-a-farewell-to-swift/\">APOD: 2026 November 6 &#8211; A Farewell to Swift</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-4-the-not-so-hidden-galaxy-ic-342/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-6-a-farewell-to-swift/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nJerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. Today\u2019s image peers through the plane of the Milky Way, through all its gas, dust and stars, to unveil this spiral galaxy. IC 342 (or Caldwell 5) is one of the brightest members of the IC 342/Maffei group of galaxies. Located about 10 million light years away, this group is quite close to the Local Group that includes our Milky Way. Inaccurate accounting of the crowded and dusty Milky Way foreground has led to misunderstandings in IC 342\u2019s history, including the theory that the galaxy was ejected from the Local Group. IC 342 has its own dust intermittently blocking the glow of hydrogen gas, indicating the presence of bright, young stars. Located about 10 million <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanets/what-is-a-light-year/\">light years</a> away, this group is quite close to the <a href=\"https://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/features/cosmic/local_group_info.html\">Local Group</a> that includes our Milky Way. Inaccurate accounting of the crowded and dusty Milky Way foreground has led to misunderstandings in IC 342\u2019s history, including the theory that the galaxy was <a href=\"https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1993AJ....105..886V\">ejected from the Local Group</a>. IC 342 has its own dust intermittently blocking the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-january-30-hydrogen-clouds-of-m33/\">glow of hydrogen gas</a>, indicating the presence of bright, young stars. <a href=\"https://www.mpg.de/9283089/magnetic-field-galaxy-IC342\">Magnetic field maps</a> of IC 342 reveal that magnetic fields may contribute substantially to one of the biggest galactic puzzles: <a href=\"https://www.universetoday.com/articles/astronomers-are-still-trying-to-understand-how-a-galaxys-spiral-arms-form\">how do spiral arms form</a>?<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's And to be clear, the\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/p/DXcM2fhDcSA/\">pictured comet</a>\u00a0is far behind the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-november-27-the-meteor-and-the-comet/\">streaking meteor</a>. Comet\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-april-14-the-long-wispy-tail-of-comet-r3-panstarrs/\">C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS)</a>\u00a0was captured from\u00a0<a href=\"https://youtu.be/iGdY96A0TUE\">Hautacam</a>,\u00a0<a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France\">France</a>\u00a0in April when the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2010-january-4-comet-halleys-nucleus-an-orbiting-iceberg/\">giant space iceberg</a>\u00a0sported impressive\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-october-6-the-changing-ion-tail-of-comet-lemmon/\">ion</a>\u00a0(blue) and dust\u00a0<a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/comets/en/anatomy-of-a-comet.en.jpg\">tails</a>. Sand-sized rocky debris that enters\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/general/what-is-earths-atmosphere/\">Earth\u2019s atmosphere</a>\u00a0typically appears as\u00a0<a href=\"https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/sb/meteor_streams.html\">meteors</a>, while the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-july-24-chemicals-glow-as-a-meteor-disintegrates/\">colorful foreground streak</a>\u00a0here may indicate a complicated composition. This month three\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.amsmeteors.org/calendar/\">notable meteor showers</a>\u00a0will reach their peaks. Over the next few days, the Southern\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/watch-the-skies/2015/10/26/the-taurid-swarm-is-upon-us/\">Taurids</a>\u00a0will be reaching their apex, while the Northern\u00a0<a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taurids\">Taurids</a>\u00a0will top out about a week later. Both originate from\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2003-december-23-comet-encke-returns/\">Comet 2P/Encke</a>. November is most famous for the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/leonids/\">Leonids Meteor Shower</a>, though, which originates from\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2002-november-16-tempel-tuttle-the-leonid-comet/\">Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle</a>\u00a0and will\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.reddit.com/r/WhatsWrongWithYourCat/comments/1xioc6j/cat_wont_sleep_in_his_bed_chooses_the_weirdest/#lightbox\">reach its crescendo</a>\u00a0in about two weeks.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:\u00a0</strong>a hidden gem","credit":"<a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/eddy_metais_photo/\">Eddy Metais</a>","copyright":"<a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/eddy_metais_photo/\">Eddy Metais</a>","alt":"A comet with a long flowing tail is seen below a star-filled  sky and above a peaked hill.
