Probably not. Although many\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/facts/\">meteors</a>\u00a0do originate from comets, there are\u00a0<a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_periodic_comets\">thousands</a>\u00a0of\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/comets/\">comets</a>\u00a0that have visited the inner\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/\">Solar System</a>\u00a0recently, and matching meteors to them can be tricky. And to be clear, the\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.instagram.com/p/DXcM2fhDcSA/\">pictured comet</a>\u00a0is far behind the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-november-27-the-meteor-and-the-comet/\">streaking meteor</a>. Comet\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-april-14-the-long-wispy-tail-of-comet-r3-panstarrs/\">C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS)</a>\u00a0was captured from\u00a0<a href=\"https://youtu.be/iGdY96A0TUE\">Hautacam</a>,\u00a0<a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France\">France</a>\u00a0in April when the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2010-january-4-comet-halleys-nucleus-an-orbiting-iceberg/\">giant space iceberg</a>\u00a0sported impressive\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-october-6-the-changing-ion-tail-of-comet-lemmon/\">ion</a>\u00a0(blue) and dust\u00a0<a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/comets/en/anatomy-of-a-comet.en.jpg\">tails</a>. Sand-sized rocky debris that enters\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/general/what-is-earths-atmosphere/\">Earth\u2019s atmosphere</a>\u00a0typically appears as\u00a0<a href=\"https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/sb/meteor_streams.html\">meteors</a>, while the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-july-24-chemicals-glow-as-a-meteor-disintegrates/\">colorful foreground streak</a>\u00a0here may indicate a complicated composition. This month three\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.amsmeteors.org/calendar/\">notable meteor showers</a>\u00a0will reach their peaks. Over the next few days, the Southern\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/watch-the-skies/2015/10/26/the-taurid-swarm-is-upon-us/\">Taurids</a>\u00a0will be reaching their apex, while the Northern\u00a0<a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taurids\">Taurids</a>\u00a0will top out about a week later. Both originate from\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2003-december-23-comet-encke-returns/\">Comet 2P/Encke</a>. November is most famous for the\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/leonids/\">Leonids Meteor Shower</a>, though, which originates from\u00a0<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2002-november-16-tempel-tuttle-the-leonid-comet/\">Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle</a>\u00a0and will\u00a0<a href=\"https://www.reddit.com/r/WhatsWrongWithYourCat/comments/1xioc6j/cat_wont_sleep_in_his_bed_chooses_the_weirdest/#lightbox\">reach its crescendo</a>\u00a0in about two weeks.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:\u00a0</strong>a hidden gem\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-4-the-not-so-hidden-galaxy-ic-342/\">APOD: 2026 November 4 &#8211; The cloud forms only during spring and summer seasons and then only during morning hours. Made of water-ice, the most familiar process that causes cloud crystals to form around bits of dust would fail due to the thinness and lack of dust high in the Martian atmosphere. Leading speculation holds that dust is not involved. After the cloud forms near the volcano Arsia Mons, wind blows the cloud downstream \u2014 creating a tail that can extend over 1500 kilometers. Efforts to better understand AMECs will continue, an understanding that may bolster a more complete view of cloud formation on Earth.Tomorrow&#039;s picture: eyeing a cat\">\n<!-- -->\n<meta name=\"keywords\" content=\"a long cloud on mars\">\n<meta property=\"og:type\" content=\"article\">\n<meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"A Long Cloud on Mars\">\n<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-2-a-long-cloud-on-mars/\">\n<meta property=\"og:site_name\" content=\"NASA Science\">\n<meta property=\"og:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/MonsCloud_MarsExpress_1920.jpg?w=1920&#038;h=1200&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:secure_url\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/MonsCloud_MarsExpress_1920.jpg?w=1920&#038;h=1200&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:alt\" content=\"Mars is seen from orbit with an orange landscape and two prominent volcanoes on the right. Cowart</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> What\u2019s causing this unusually long cloud on <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mars/\">Mars</a>?\u00a0Known as the <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Mars_Express/Mars_s_oddest_cloud_may_be_even_odder_than_we_thought\">Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud</a> (AMEC) and first recorded by NASA\u2019s <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/viking-2/\">Viking Orbiter 2</a> in 1977, the <a href=\"https://www.universetoday.com/articles/marss-most-mysterious-cloud-might-be-defying-textbook-cloud-physics\">strange cloud</a> has been imaged in greater detail more recently by <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/\">ESA</a>\u2019s robotic <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Mars_Express\">Mars Express</a> spacecraft.\u00a0The <a href=\"https://www.flickr.com/photos/132160802@N06/49046308893/\">featured</a> <a href=\"https://www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Images/2026/10/The_Arsia_Mons_Elongated_Cloud_as_seen_by_Mars_Express\">image</a> is from 2018. The <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/kids/earth/how-do-clouds-form/\">cloud forms</a> only during <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-march-20-spring-equinox-at-teide-observatory/\">spring</a> and summer <a href=\"https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/seasons/\">seasons</a> and then only during morning hours. Made of water-ice, the most familiar process that causes <a href=\"https://airbornescience.nasa.gov/content/Sampling_the_composition_of_cirrus_ice_residuals\">cloud crystals</a> to <a href=\"https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/10387\">form around bits of dust</a> would fail due to the thinness and lack of dust high in the <a href=\"https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/mars-atmosphere-equation-english/\">Martian atmosphere</a>. <a href=\"https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-026-02089-9\">Leading speculation</a> holds that dust is not involved. After the cloud forms near the volcano <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsia_Mons\">Arsia Mons</a>, wind blows the cloud <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2012-april-22-flowing-barchan-sand-dunes-on-mars/\">downstream</a> \u2014 creating a tail that can extend over 1500 kilometers. Efforts to better understand <a href=\"https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2020JE006517\">AMEC</a>s will continue, an understanding that may bolster a <a href=\"https://unsplash.com/photos/brown-tabby-cat-7GX5aICb5i4\">more complete view</a> of <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/kids/earth/how-do-clouds-form/\">cloud formation</a> on <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/\">Earth</a>.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture:</strong> eyeing a cat\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-3-comet-panstarrs-and-rainbow-meteor/\">APOD: 2026 November 3 &#8211; Comet PanSTARRs and Rainbow Meteor</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-1-colors-of-the-moon/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-3-comet-panstarrs-and-rainbow-meteor/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nRobert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. U.</a><br>\n</center>\n</body>\n</html>","basic_html_url":"https://science.nasa.gov/wp-json/wp/v2/apod-basic/261102/html"},{"date":"2026-11-01","post_id":1507027,"title":"Colors of the Moon","permalink":"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-1-colors-of-the-moon/","media_type":"image","explanation":"<strong>Explanation:</strong> What color is the Moon? It depends on the night -- and the time. Outside of the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-atmosphere/earths-atmosphere-a-multi-layered-cake/\">Earth's atmosphere</a>, the <a href=\"https://www.universetoday.com/articles/moon-albedo\">dark Moon</a>, which shines by reflected sunlight, appears a <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2003-november-9-apollo-17-lunarscape-a-magnificent-desolation/\">magnificent</a>ly brown-tinged gray. The <a href=\"https://greenflash.photo/portfolio/colors-of-the-moon/\">featured image</a> highlights a collection of apparent colors of the full moon on Earth, documented by one astrophotographer over 10 years from <a href=\"https://youtu.be/G0EUqGhYZ6Y\">different locations</a> across <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy\">Italy</a>. A <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2022-november-11-blood-moon-ice-giant/\">red</a>- or <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-january-20-io-in-true-color/\">yellow</a>-colored moon usually indicates a moon seen <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod/apod-2026-august-1-buck-moon-and-belt-of-venus/\">near the horizon</a>. There, some of the blue light has been scattered away by a long path through the <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/general/what-is-earths-atmosphere/\">Earth's atmosphere</a>, sometimes laden with fine dust. A <a href=\"https://www.loc.gov/everyday-mysteries/categories/astronomy/item/what-is-a-blue-moon-is-it-ever-really-blue/\">blue-colored moon</a> is more rare and can indicate an atmosphere carrying larger <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/a-dusty-journey-146122/\">dust particles</a>. What created the purple moon is <a href=\"https://cdn.akc.org/content/hero/bulldog_rib_bone_hero.jpg\">unclear</a> -- it may be a combination of several effects. The last image captures the total <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-march-7-two-eclipses-of-saros-133/\">lunar eclipse</a> of 2018 July -- where the moon, in <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-august-25-earths-shadow-visualized-with-lunar-eclipses/\">Earth's shadow</a>, appeared a faint red -- due to light <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refraction\">refracted</a> through air around the Earth. <a href=\"https://asterisk.apod.com/discuss_apod.php?date=261101\">Have you</a> ever seen an unusually colorful Moon?<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong><a href=\"https://apod.com/fap/ap261102.html\">open space</a>","credit":"<a href=\"https://greenflash.photo/about-me/\">Marcella Giulia Pace</a>","copyright":"<a href=\"https://greenflash.photo/about-me/\">Marcella Giulia Pace</a>","alt":"Different colored images of the Moon are arranged in a spiral pattern.","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-1-colors-of-the-moon/","hdurl":"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/november/MoonColors_Pace_960.jpg?w=960&h=991&fit=clip","basic_html":"<!doctype html>\n<html>\n<head>\n<meta charset=\"UTF-8\">\n<meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">\n<title> APOD: 2026 November 1 - Colors of the Moon</title>\n<link rel=\"canonical\" href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-1-colors-of-the-moon/\">\n<!-- gsfc meta tags -->\n<meta name=\"orgcode\" content=\"661\">\n<meta name=\"rno\" content=\"Dana Bolles\">\n<meta name=\"content-owner\" content=\"Robert Nemiroff\">\n<meta name=\"webmaster\" content=\"Stephen.F.Fantasia.1\">\n<meta name=\"description\" content=\"Explanation: What color is the Moon? It depends on the night -- and the time. Outside of the Earth&#039;s atmosphere, the dark Moon, which shines by reflected sunlight, appears a magnificently brown-tinged gray. The featured image highlights a collection of apparent colors of the full moon on Earth, documented by one astrophotographer over 10 years from different locations across Italy. A red- or yellow-colored moon usually indicates a moon seen near the horizon. There, some of the blue light has been scattered away by a long path through the Earth&#039;s atmosphere, sometimes laden with fine dust. A blue-colored moon is more rare and can indicate an atmosphere carrying larger dust particles. What created the purple moon is unclear -- it may be a combination of several effects. The last image captures the total lunar eclipse of 2018 July -- where the moon, in Earth&#039;s shadow, appeared a faint red -- due to light refracted through air around the Earth. text=\"#000000\" link=\"#0000FF\" vlink=\"#7F0F9F\"\nalink=\"#FF0000\">\n\n<center>\n<h1> Astronomy Picture of the Day </h1>\n<p>\n\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Discover the href=\"https://greenflash.photo/about-me/\">Marcella Giulia Pace</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> What color is the Moon? It depends on the night -- and the time. Outside of the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-atmosphere/earths-atmosphere-a-multi-layered-cake/\">Earth's atmosphere</a>, the <a href=\"https://www.universetoday.com/articles/moon-albedo\">dark Moon</a>, which shines by reflected sunlight, appears a <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2003-november-9-apollo-17-lunarscape-a-magnificent-desolation/\">magnificent</a>ly brown-tinged gray. The <a href=\"https://greenflash.photo/portfolio/colors-of-the-moon/\">featured image</a> highlights a collection of apparent colors of the full moon on Earth, documented by one astrophotographer over 10 years from <a href=\"https://youtu.be/G0EUqGhYZ6Y\">different locations</a> across <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy\">Italy</a>. A <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2022-november-11-blood-moon-ice-giant/\">red</a>- or <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-january-20-io-in-true-color/\">yellow</a>-colored moon usually indicates a moon seen <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod/apod-2026-august-1-buck-moon-and-belt-of-venus/\">near the horizon</a>. There, some of the blue light has been scattered away by a long path through the <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/general/what-is-earths-atmosphere/\">Earth's atmosphere</a>, sometimes laden with fine dust. A <a href=\"https://www.loc.gov/everyday-mysteries/categories/astronomy/item/what-is-a-blue-moon-is-it-ever-really-blue/\">blue-colored moon</a> is more rare and can indicate an atmosphere carrying larger <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/a-dusty-journey-146122/\">dust particles</a>. What created the purple moon is <a href=\"https://cdn.akc.org/content/hero/bulldog_rib_bone_hero.jpg\">unclear</a> -- it may be a combination of several effects. The last image captures the total <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-march-7-two-eclipses-of-saros-133/\">lunar eclipse</a> of 2018 July -- where the moon, in <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-august-25-earths-shadow-visualized-with-lunar-eclipses/\">Earth's shadow</a>, appeared a faint red -- due to light <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refraction\">refracted</a> through air around the Earth. <a href=\"https://asterisk.apod.com/discuss_apod.php?date=261101\">Have you</a> ever seen an unusually colorful Moon?<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong><a href=\"https://apod.com/fap/ap261102.html\">open space</a>\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-2-a-long-cloud-on-mars/\">APOD: 2026 November 2 &#8211; href=\"https://www.facebook.com/stephane.vetter.nuitsacrees\">St\u00e9phane Vetter</a> (<a href=\"http://www.nuitsacrees.fr/\">Nuits sacr\u00e9es</a>)\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/sinister-solar-system/\">What spooky planet is this?</a> Planet Earth on a dark and stormy night, of course. The ghostly scene was <a href=\"https://twanight.org/gallery/night-on-a-spooky-planet/\">photographed at Hverir</a>, a geothermally active area found along northeastern Iceland's <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krafla\">volcanic landscape</a>. Triggered by <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/sun/solar-storms-and-flares/\">solar activity</a>, <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/johnson/halloween-aboard-the-international-space-station/\">geomagnetic storms</a> have unleashed energetic particles trapped in Earth's magnetic field. Penetrating the planet's upper atmosphere at high latitudes, the particles create <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/sun/auroras/\">auroral displays</a> in the starry night sky. Ghostly towers of steam and gas are venting from <a href=\"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oWjdXf67dLQ\">local fumaroles to dance</a> against the eerie, greenish northern lights. For now, auroral activity on planet Earth remains in a high state as the Sun is only in early phases of decline from the peak of its <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_maximum\">solar activity cycle</a>. And soon, other ghostly apparitions may dance in your neighborhood. <a href=\"https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/johnson/halloween-aboard-the-international-space-station/\">Happy Halloween</a>!<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>many moons\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-1-colors-of-the-moon/\">APOD: 2026 November 1 \u2013 Colors of the Moon</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-october-30-haunting-the-cepheus-flare/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-november-1-colors-of-the-moon/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nJerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. Of course, <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2021-october-30-a-rorschach-aurora/\">the shapes</a> are cosmic dust clouds visible in dimly reflected starlight. Far from <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/stories/\">your own neighborhood</a>, they lurk above the plane of the Milky Way at the edge of the <a href=\"http://arxiv.org/abs/0809.4761\">Cepheus Flare</a> molecular cloud complex some 1,200 light-years away. Over 2 light-years across and brighter than most of the other ghostly apparitions, vdB 141 or Sh2-136 is also known as the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=111031\">Ghost Nebula</a>. It lies at lower right in the starry field of view. Inside the Ghost Nebula are reddish telltale signs of dense cores collapsing in the early stages <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/science-highlights/exploring-the-birth-of-stars/\">of star formation</a>. With the eerie hue of interstellar dust reflecting bluish light from hot young stars of <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=210903\">NGC 7023, the Iris Nebula</a> stands out against the dark just left of center. <a href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/u/mirko75?i=20obtn\">In the broad telescopic frame</a>, these fertile interstellar dust fields stretch almost six full moons across the sky.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>night on a spooky planet","credit":"<a href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/u/mirko75\">Mirko Tondinelli</a>","copyright":"<a href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/u/mirko75\">Mirko Tondinelli</a>","alt":"Interstellar dust clouds and dark nebulae in the Cepheus molecular cloud.","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-october-30-haunting-the-cepheus-flare/","hdurl":"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/october/CepheusFlare_Tondinelli.jpg?w=6000&h=4076&fit=clip","basic_html":"<!doctype html>\n<html>\n<head>\n<meta charset=\"UTF-8\">\n<meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">\n<title> APOD: 2026 October 30 - Haunting the Cepheus Flare</title>\n<link rel=\"canonical\" href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-october-30-haunting-the-cepheus-flare/\">\n<!-- gsfc meta tags -->\n<meta name=\"orgcode\" content=\"661\">\n<meta name=\"rno\" content=\"Dana Bolles\">\n<meta name=\"content-owner\" content=\"Robert Nemiroff\">\n<meta name=\"webmaster\" content=\"Stephen.F.Fantasia.1\">\n<meta name=\"description\" content=\"Explanation: Spooky shapes seem to haunt this dusty expanse, drifting through the night in the royal constellation Cepheus. Of course, the shapes are cosmic dust clouds visible in dimly reflected starlight. Far from your own neighborhood, they lurk above the plane of the Milky Way at the edge of the Cepheus Flare molecular cloud complex some 1,200 light-years away. Over 2 light-years across and brighter than most of the other ghostly apparitions, vdB 141 or Sh2-136 is also known as the Ghost Nebula. It lies at lower right in the starry field of view. Inside the Ghost Nebula are reddish telltale signs of dense cores collapsing in the early stages of star formation. With the eerie hue of interstellar dust reflecting bluish light from hot young stars of NGC 7023, the Iris Nebula stands out against the dark just left of center. SRC=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/october/CepheusFlare_Tondinelli.jpg\" alt=\"Interstellar dust clouds and dark nebulae in the Cepheus molecular href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/u/mirko75\">Mirko Tondinelli</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> <a href=\"https://exoplanets.nasa.gov/alien-worlds/galaxy-of-horrors/\">Spooky</a> shapes seem to haunt this dusty expanse, drifting through the night in the royal constellation <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cepheus_(constellation)\">Cepheus</a>. Of course, <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2021-october-30-a-rorschach-aurora/\">the shapes</a> are cosmic dust clouds visible in dimly reflected starlight. Far from <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/stories/\">your own neighborhood</a>, they lurk above the plane of the Milky Way at the edge of the <a href=\"http://arxiv.org/abs/0809.4761\">Cepheus Flare</a> molecular cloud complex some 1,200 light-years away. Over 2 light-years across and brighter than most of the other ghostly apparitions, vdB 141 or Sh2-136 is also known as the <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=111031\">Ghost Nebula</a>. It lies at lower right in the starry field of view. Inside the Ghost Nebula are reddish telltale signs of dense cores collapsing in the early stages <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/science-highlights/exploring-the-birth-of-stars/\">of star formation</a>. With the eerie hue of interstellar dust reflecting bluish light from hot young stars of <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/?date=210903\">NGC 7023, the Iris Nebula</a> stands out against the dark just left of center. <a href=\"https://app.astrobin.com/u/mirko75?i=20obtn\">In the broad telescopic frame</a>, these fertile interstellar dust fields stretch almost six full moons across the sky.<br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>night on a spooky planet\n<p> <center>\n\n<b> Tomorrow's picture: </b><a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-october-31-night-on-a-spooky-planet/\">APOD: 2026 October 31 \u2013 Night on a Spooky Planet</a>\n\n<p> <hr>\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-29-october-2026-the-horns-of-venus/\">&lt;</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Archive</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Index</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Search</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/calendar/\">Calendar</a>\n| <a href=\"/feed/apod-basic/\">RSS</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/education-links/\">Education</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">About APOD</a>\n| <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-october-31-night-on-a-spooky-planet/\">&gt;</a>\n\n<hr><p>\n<b> Authors & editors: </b>\nJerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Keighley Rockcliffe<br>\n<b>NASA Official: </b> Dana Bolles<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Specific rights apply</a>.<br>\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/about/highlights/HP_Privacy.html\">NASA Web\nPrivacy Policy and Important Notices</a><br>\n<b>A service of:</b>\n<a href=\"http://astrophysics.gsfc.nasa.gov/\">ASD</a> at\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/\">NASA</a> /\n<a href=\"http://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/\">GSFC</a>\n<br><b>&</b> <a href=\"http://www.mtu.edu/\">Michigan Tech. But you could be forgiven for thinking it was a crescent Moon in the sky. It is a lesser known fact that Venus also has phases. (What about other planets?) The featured image shows Venus seen almost directly between the Sun and the Earth. This happens once every year and a half, and it is like the alignment that happens every month during a new Moon. But the new Moon is dark, while Venus&#039; backlit atmosphere refracts and scatters the sunlight, creating a glowing crescent arc that extends beyond 180 degrees: the tips of this arc are called the &quot;horns&quot;. The crescent can be seen with a small telescope or binoculars during twilight, but those with exceptionally acute eyesight may be able to see it with the unaided eye. Ancient Babylonian astronomers may have been the first to study Venus&#039; brightness changes, which are related to its phases. Many other cultures have similar astronomical records, including the oldest surviving Maya book. Tomorrow&#039;s picture: a cosmic haunting\">\n<!-- -->\n<meta name=\"keywords\" content=\"the horns of venus\">\n<meta property=\"og:type\" content=\"article\">\n<meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"The Horns of Venus\">\n<meta property=\"og:url\" content=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-29-october-2026-the-horns-of-venus/\">\n<meta property=\"og:site_name\" content=\"NASA Science\">\n<meta property=\"og:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/october/venus_20261024a.jpg?w=744&#038;h=744&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:secure_url\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/october/venus_20261024a.jpg?w=744&#038;h=744&#038;fit=clip\">\n<meta property=\"og:image:alt\" content=\"See Explanation.  Clicking on the picture will download the highest resolution version available.\">\n<meta property=\"article:published_time\" content=\"2026-10-29T00:05:00-04:00\">\n<meta property=\"article:modified_time\" content=\"2026-10-29T17:02:05-04:00\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:card\" content=\"summary_large_image\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:title\" content=\"The Horns of Venus\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:site\" content=\"@NASA\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:creator\" content=\"@NASA\">\n<meta name=\"twitter:image\" content=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/october/venus_20261024a.jpg?w=744&#038;h=744&#038;fit=clip\">\n</head>\n<body BGCOLOR=\"#F4F4FF\" text=\"#000000\" link=\"#0000FF\" vlink=\"#7F0F9F\"\nalink=\"#FF0000\">\n\n<center>\n<h1> Astronomy Picture of the Day </h1>\n<p>\n\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/archive/\">Discover the cosmos!</a>\nEach day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is\nfeatured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.\n<p>\n\n2026 October 29<br>\n\n<a href=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/october/venus_20261024a.jpg\">\n<IMG SRC=\"https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/apod/apod/2026/october/venus_20261024a.jpg\" alt=\"See Explanation.  Clicking on the picture will download the highest resolution version available.\"></a>\n</center>\n\n<center>\n<b> The Horns of Venus </b> <br>\n\n<b>Image Credit &\n<a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/apod/about-apod/\">Copyright</a>:</b>\n\n<a href=\"http://www.astrophoto.fr/\">Thierry Legault</a>\n</center>\n\n<p>\n\n<b> Explanation: </b>\n\n<strong>Explanation:</strong> <a href=\"https://tenor.com/view/thats-no-moon-obi-wan-kenobi-starwars-death-star-gif-10170550\">That's no moon.</a> But you could be forgiven for thinking it was a <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/moon/moon-phases/\">crescent Moon</a> in the sky. It is a lesser known fact that <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phases_of_Venus\">Venus also has phases</a>. (What about <a href=\"https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~blackman/ast104/aspects6.html\">other planets?</a>) The <a href=\"http://www.astrophoto.fr/20261024_venus_inferior_conjunction.html\">featured image</a> shows <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/venus/\">Venus</a> seen almost directly between the Sun and the Earth. This happens once every <a href=\"https://astro.dur.ac.uk/~ams/users/inner_rest.html\">year and a half</a>, and it is like the alignment that happens every month during a new Moon. But the new Moon is dark, while Venus' backlit <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-july-3-venus-in-ultraviolet-from-akatsuki/\">atmosphere</a> <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/ems/03_behaviors/\">refracts and scatters</a> the sunlight, creating a glowing <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2023-august-26-crescents-of-venus/\">crescent arc</a> that extends beyond 180 degrees: the tips of this arc are called the \"horns\". The crescent can be seen with a small telescope or binoculars during twilight, but those with <a href=\"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1497119146420-012f8fc80a3a\">exceptionally acute eyesight</a> may be able to see it with the unaided eye. Ancient <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_tablet_of_Ammisaduqa\">Babylonian</a> astronomers may have been the first to study Venus' brightness changes, which are related to its <a href=\"https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-january-8-the-phases-of-venus/\">phases</a>. <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_in_culture\">Many other cultures</a> have similar astronomical records, including the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden_Codex\">oldest </a><a href=\"https://www.loc.gov/resource/gdcwdl.wdl_11621/?st=gallery\">surviving</a><a         									<h1 class="display-48 margin-top-0 margin-bottom-3">De Gerlache-Kocher Massif</h1>
        					
        					<div class="grid-row media-detail-hero__content-row">
        									<div class="grid-col-12 desktop:grid-col-6">
        						<p class="p-md margin-0 media-detail-hero__description">
        							<strong>Explanation:</strong> De Gerlache-Kocher <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif">massif</a> looms on the visible horizon in this close-up of the edge of the Moon. The mountainous formation rises about 4 kilometers above its surroundings and is located very close to the lunar south pole. Boasting <a href="https://lroc.im-ldi.com/images/271">permanently shadowed</a> crater floors that likely contain deposits of water ice and peaks that receive almost continuous sunlight for solar power generation, the south polar region is <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase/">considered a prime location</a> for the first human settlement on the Moon. <a href="https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023LPICo2989.2037E/abstract">In fact</a>, De Gerlache-Kocher massif itself has been considered as a potential <a href="https://www.universetoday.com/articles/nasa-narrows-artemis-landing-sites-to-9-key-regions">landing site</a> for future crewed <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-iv/">Artemis missions to the Moon</a>. The remarkable telescopic image of the massif at the lunar limb was captured on October 31. Then, a favorable libration angle or <a href="https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/10836/">lunar wobble</a> enhanced this oblique view <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-august-30-southern-moonscape/">across the Moon's south pole.</a><br><br><strong>Tomorrow's picture: </strong>meteoric						</p>
        					</div>

        <body class="html front not-logged-in page-indexhtml page-home">
           <a class="accessible" href="#content" style="display: none; visibility: hidden;">[Skip to Content]</a>
           <div align="center">
              <header id="section-header" class="section section-header">
                 <div id="section-header-menu-container"></div>
              </header>
              <main>
                 <a id="content"></a>
                 <div class="box">
                 <div class="body">
                    <p>
                       <div class="mainimg">
                          <img src="/img/api.png" alt="NASA Technology Transfer API" title="NASA Technology Transfer API" class="rounded">
                       </div>
                       <h1 class="featuretitle">Technology Transfer API</h1>
                       <h2 style="font-size: 24px;">Build with us</h2>
                       <p>
                          Technology transfer builds commercial activity, encourages economic growth, 
                          and stimulates innovation in business and commerce. Our transferrable technologies 
                          are made open to allow innovations that benefit the public and stimulate economic development. 
                          <br><br>
                          As a developer, you can now use our available API to build and integrate
                          your services with the Agency's Technology Transfer Program's abundant data resources.
                          <br><br>
                          Take a look at some products built on our API:
                          <ul>
                             <li><a href="https://technology.nasa.gov" target="_blank">Technology Tranfer Portal</a></li>
                             <li><a href="http://software.nasa.gov" target="_blank">Software Catalog</a></li>
                             <li><a href="http://spinoff.nasa.gov" target="_blank">Spinoff</a></li>
                          </ul>
                       </p>
                    </p>
                    <h2 style="font-size: 24px;">Our Data</h2>
                    <p class="about">
                       <strong>Patent Portfolio</strong>
                       <br>
                       <img src="https://technology.nasa.gov/img/patent.png" style="width: 150px;" alt="NASA Technology Transfer API" title="NASA Technology Transfer API" class="rounded">
                       The NASA patent portfolio is available to benefit US citizens. Through partnerships
                       and licensing agreements with industry, these patents ensure that NASA investments
                       in pioneering research find secondary uses that benefit the economy, create jobs, and
                       improve quality of life. Our patent portfolio contains over 1400 technologies
                       currently available for licensing.
                    </p>
                    <p class="about">
                       <strong>Software Catalog</strong>
                       <br>
                       <img src="https://technology.nasa.gov/img/SoftwareCat.icon.png" style="width: 150px;" alt="NASA Technology Transfer API" title="NASA Technology Transfer API" class="rounded">
                       Offering an extensive portfolio of software products for a wide variety of technical
                       applications, the NASA Software Catalog is organized into fifteen broad subject matter
                       categories.  All catalog entries include the software title, the product ID number
                       (known internally as the NASA case number), a short description, and the software's
                       specified release type. Some software descriptions contain links to additional
                       information or downloading options. 
                    </p>
                    <p class="about">
                       <strong>Spinoff</strong>
                       <br>
                       <img src="https://technology.nasa.gov/img/spinoff-2015.jpg" style="width: 150px;" alt="NASA Technology Transfer API" title="NASA Technology Transfer API" class="rounded">
                       NASA's Spinoff publication accomplishes several goals. First, it is a convincing
                       justification for the continued expenditure of NASA funds. It serves as a tool to
                       educate the media and the general public by informing them about the benefits and
                       dispelling the myth of wasted taxpayer dollars. It reinforces interest in space
                       exploration. It demonstrates the possibility to apply aerospace technology in
                       different environments. It highlights the ingenuity of American inventors,
                       entrepreneurs, and application engineers, and the willingness of a government
                       agency to assist them. And finally, it continues to ensure global competitiveness
                       and technological leadership by the United States.
                    </p>
                    
                    <br clear="all">
                    <h2 style="font-size: 24px;">Build on our API</h2>
                    <p>
                       The T2 API is designed around REST (Representational State Transfer) and responses
                       are available in JSON format.
                    </p>
                    <p>
                       Simply build your data query using the following url syntax:
                       <div class="code">
                          <pre>
        https://technology.nasa.gov/api/api/[ patent | software | spinoff ]/{ keywords }
                          </pre>
                       </div>
                    </p>
                    <p>
                       Query examples:
                       <div class="code">
                          <pre>
        https://technology.nasa.gov/api/api/patent/rocket
        
        https://technology.nasa.gov/api/api/software/visualization

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=edge"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><link rel="shortcut icon" href="favicon.ico"><script src="lib/jquery/jquery.min.js"></script><script src="lib/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.js"></script><script src="js/trekApi.js"></script><link rel="stylesheet" href="lib/bootstrap/bootstrap.min.css"><link rel="stylesheet" href="css/trekAPI.css"></head><body><div class="container-fluid" id="introContainer"><div class="topNavigatorDiv"><ul class="navList"><li><a href="index.html">TREK MAP SERVICES</a></li><li><a href="#description">DESCRIPTION</a></li><li><a href="#services">SERVICES</a></li><li><a href="https://trek.nasa.gov"><span class="homeSite">SOLAR SYSTEM TREKS</span></a></li></ul></div><div class="row"><div class="introLogo h1Top"><img class="nasaLogoLarge" src="assets/nasa-logo-large.png"></div></div><div class="row"><h1 class="h1Center lightWeight"></h1></div><div class="row"><h1 class="h1Center"><span class="mainSubtitle">WMTS Layer Services</span></h1></div></div><a name="description"></a><div class="container-fluid contentContainer"><button class="subHeader" data-toggle="collapse" data-target="#desContent" onclick="this.blur();">Description</button><div class="collapse in" id="desContent"><p>Map layers are available through the OGC RESTful WMTS protocol. To find out more information about OGC WMTS, go to <a href="https://www.opengeospatial.org/standards/wmts">https://www.opengeospatial.org/standards/wmts</a>. A simple javascript example using ESRI javascript client library is included for each service. Click 'Preview' to run it.</p><p>To access these tiles through a WMTS client library, depending on the WMTS client library, you only need to provide the WMTS Endpoint and the full extent or bbox information. However, if you want to access tiles without using a WMTS client library, the following information will give you some help.</p><p>Here is basic information about how to request image tiles from a RESTful WMTS service. The basic URL template is as follows:</p><pre> https://{WMTS endpoint}/1.0.0/{Style}/{TileMatrixSet}/{TileMatrix}/{TileRow}/{TileCol}.png</pre><p>* Some services are .png and some are .jpg. Please look at WMTS GetCapabilities ResourcesURL element to find out what extension to use.</p><p>In order to fill in the variables in the template URL, you need to parse the WMTS GetCapabilities XML. GetCapabilities XML can be found for each product below.</p><p>From the WMTS GetCapabilities XML, find ows:Identifier element inside Style element. This value replaces {Style}. The ows:Identifier element inside TileMatrixSet element replaces {TileMatrixSet}. Inside the TileMatrixSet element in WMTS Capabilities, there is a list of TileMatrix. This is the Zoom level. Replace {TileMatrix} with the ows:Identifier found in TileMatrix element.</p><p>{TileRow} and {TileCol} are row and col index for tiles. The first zoom level for a product that covers the entire globe will have two columns and one row so that the URLs are as follows:</p><pre id="wmtsSample1"></pre><pre id="wmtsSample2"></pre><p>The second zoom level has four columns and two rows and so on.</p><p>If the image tile is missing, that means there is no data coverage in that area. You can also use coverage Bbox to calculate the coverage before requesting image tiles.</p></div><button class="subHeader" data-toggle="collapse" data-target="#serviceContent" onclick="this.blur();">Service</button> <a name="services"></a><div class="collapse in" id="serviceContent"><div class="projTabs"><div class="tabDiv" id="eq">Equirectangular</div><div class="tabDiv" id="np">North Pole</div><div class="tabDiv" id="sp">South Pole</div></div><br><div class="subTab" id="eqTab"><h2 class="projLabel">Equirectangular</h2><hr><div id="eqLayerList" class="layerList"></div></div><div class="subTab" id="npTab"><h2 class="projLabel">North Pole</h2><hr><div id="npLayerList" class="layerList"></div></div><div class="subTab" id="spTab"><h2 class="projLabel">South Pole</h2><hr><div id="spLayerList" class="layerList"></div></div></div></div><div class="container-fluid footerContainer"><br><footer class="footer"><p id="footerPara">&copy; 2016 Trek</p></footer></div></body></html>
